title: The Sports Nutrition Market: A Brand's Read
summary: The sports nutrition market: how the category moved from specialty into grocery and convenience, and how to read active nutrition in your own data.
body_markdown:
The sports nutrition market used to mean powders sold to serious lifters in specialty stores. It now means protein bars in a grocery checkout lane, RTD shakes in a convenience cooler, and functional powders in the wellness set, sold largely to people who do not consider themselves athletes.


That shift, usually labeled active nutrition, is the most important fact about the category, and it breaks most of the measurement a brand inherits.


## Key takeaways


- The buyer moved from athletes to mainstream shoppers, which changed the channel, the pack, and the price point.
- Category boundaries are genuinely blurry. Your competitive set may include snack bars and energy drinks that no report classifies with you.
- Ecommerce carries a large share of powder volume and is invisible in store-level syndicated data.
- Protein claims have proliferated far faster than the demand behind any individual one. Test the claim, do not assume it.


## The category-definition problem


This is the practical obstacle that costs brands the most time. A protein bar competes with sports nutrition bars, snack bars, granola bars, and meal replacement, and syndicated classification will place it in exactly one of those. Your share number depends entirely on which.


Three consequences worth planning around:


- Your reported share can move because a competitor was reclassified, with no change in anyone's sales.
- The retailer's category definition may differ from the syndicated one, so your buyer's set and your report's set are not the same items.
- Shelf adjacency tells you the truth. Whatever is physically next to you is your competitive set, regardless of classification.


The workable rule: build your own competitive set from shelf adjacency and price tier, use it for every internal read, and translate to the syndicated definition only when you need a number that matches someone else's.


## Where to get defensible numbers


Circana and NIQ for retail sales with stated market coverage. SPINS for the natural and specialty channel, which is where much of the functional end of the category still concentrates. The Council for Responsible Nutrition publishes supplement industry survey data. For anything ecommerce, the syndicated store-level sources will not help and the retailer's own reporting is the only view.


## Sports nutrition market segments that behave differently


Segment Primary channel What drives velocity


Powders Ecommerce and specialty, then club Price per serving and repeat. Trial is expensive; retention is everything.


Bars Grocery, mass, convenience Impulse and placement. Front-end and checkout placement transforms velocity.


RTD shakes Convenience and grocery cold sets Cold placement and single-serve price point.


Functional and hydration Natural, then conventional Claim credibility and a specific occasion.


The powder row carries a measurement warning. If a large share of your powder volume sells through ecommerce and subscription, a syndicated brick-and-mortar read will show a category that looks smaller and flatter than the one you are in. Brands have cut powder lines on the strength of a store-level report while the same items grew online.


## Testing a protein claim in your own data


Protein content is the category's dominant claim and the one most often assumed rather than measured. The test is the same shape as any attribute test.


- Tag your competitive set by grams of protein per serving, in bands rather than continuous values.
- Compare velocity per store per week across bands, in the same stores, holding price tier constant.
- Then check whether the higher band sustains a price premium outside promoted weeks.


A worked read: a bar brand assumed moving from 12 g to 20 g of protein would lift velocity. Across 290 stores, the 15 to 19 g band outperformed both the 10 to 14 and the 20-plus bands, and the 20-plus band sold at parity price only during promotion. The reformulation would have cost margin and taste to reach a band the shelf did not reward.


## How Scout fits


Scout lets you define the competitive set explicitly rather than inheriting a syndicated classification, which in a category this blurry is the difference between a share number you can act on and one that moves when somebody else gets reclassified. Attributes such as protein band sit alongside velocity, price, and distribution, so the claim test above is a view rather than a project.


Related:[SPINS for wellness and beauty](https://www.cpgscout.ai/learn/spins-for-wellness-beauty) and[attribute tagging](https://www.cpgscout.ai/glossary/attribute-tagging) .


## Frequently asked questions


What is active nutrition?The broader framing that replaced sports nutrition as the category moved from athletes in specialty retail to mainstream shoppers in grocery and convenience. It spans bars, RTD shakes, powders, and functional and hydration products.


Why is the category so hard to size?Category boundaries overlap with snack bars, meal replacement, and energy drinks, and syndicated classification assigns each item to one category. Your share depends on which definition is used, and it can move without any sales changing.


Does ecommerce matter for this category?Substantially, especially for powders, where subscription and online purchase carry a large share of volume that store-level syndicated data does not see at all.


Is more protein always better?No. Test it. Velocity by protein band frequently peaks in a middle range, and higher bands often sustain their price only on promotion, which means the reformulation costs margin without buying velocity.


## What a retailer is deciding when they list you


The buyer's question in this category is rarely whether your product is good. It is which of four adjacent sets your item belongs in, and whether it earns its space against the incumbents in that set. A bar can be merchandised in the nutrition set, the snack aisle, the front-end, or a wellness endcap, and the same item will produce completely different velocity in each.


That makes placement negotiation more valuable than most brands treat it. Ask where the item will physically sit before agreeing to a listing, and benchmark the velocity commitment against items in that specific location rather than against the category. A bar promised front-end placement and set in the nutrition aisle will miss a velocity target it never had a chance at, and the delisting conversation will be about the product.


The corollary for measurement: record placement alongside velocity from week one. Without it, the first performance review has no way to separate a product problem from a placement problem, and the default assumption in the room will be the product.
